intro: Hi! Today you learn how to give a friend good advice with should, and how to talk about rules and duties with have to and must. You also learn one very important difference: mustn't (dilarang) and don't have to (tidak perlu). Warm-up: how do you say 'sebaiknya kamu istirahat' in English?
teachingNotes: Stress the node's common errors and say why: *'You should to rest' -> 'You should rest' (should and must are helper words like can: no to, no -s, the base verb comes straight after them; learners add 'to' because 'have to' has one). *'She have to work on Saturday' -> 'She has to work on Saturday' (the 'have' in 'have to' is the normal verb have from the simple present: she has a car, so she has to work). *'It's a holiday tomorrow, so you mustn't come to work' -> 'you don't have to come to work'.

Indonesian mapping: should = sebaiknya / seharusnya, shouldn't = sebaiknya jangan; have to / must = harus / wajib; mustn't = dilarang / tidak boleh / jangan; don't have to = tidak perlu / tidak harus / tidak usah. The big trap: 'tidak harus' looks like 'must not' word by word, but mustn't means dilarang. Saying 'You mustn't bring anything' to a guest sounds like a ban. Also, Indonesians give friendly advice with 'harus' (Kamu harus istirahat!): in English 'You must rest' sounds strong, like a doctor's order, so friendly advice uses should. (Exception if asked: 'You must try this sate!' is a normal, friendly way to recommend something you love.)

Must vs have to: in positive sentences both mean harus and are very often both correct (You must / have to wear a helmet). Give only a simple guide: have to is the most common in speaking (jobs, timetables, rules); must is common on signs and written rules and when the speaker feels something is important (I must call my mother). Never build an exercise where the learner must choose between must and have to by meaning. Questions use Do I have to ...? (Must I ...? sounds old-fashioned).

Form: should and must never change and take no do (Should I ...? / You mustn't ...). have to behaves like a normal verb: has to with he/she/it, negatives with don't / doesn't have to, questions with Do / Does ... have to ...? Common error: *'She doesn't has to' -> 'She doesn't have to' (after doesn't the verb goes back to its base form, as in She doesn't work). Accept 'don't need to' as a natural alternative to don't have to, and can't as a natural alternative to mustn't for rules (learners know can't for rules from a1-can-ability).

Pronunciation and varieties: have to often sounds like 'HAF-ta' and has to like 'HAS-ta'; in mustn't the first t is silent ('MAS-ent'). mustn't is very common in British English; Americans mostly say must not in written rules or can't when speaking.

Limits: present only. No had to (past), will have to, going to, have got to, needn't, ought to, or must for guessing (He must be tired). If a learner asks, say these come in later lessons. Keep contexts adult and Indonesian (kantor, KRL, ojek, warung, rumah sakit).

keyPoints.title: should / shouldn't for advice
keyPoints.explanation: should + base verb gives advice (a good idea); shouldn't (= should not) + base verb says something is a bad idea. should is a helper word like can: it never changes, there's no to after it, and questions put it first with no do (Should I ...?).

examples.id: Sebaiknya kamu minum lebih banyak air.

examples.en: You shouldn't stay up late before a test.
examples.id: Sebaiknya kamu jangan begadang sebelum ujian.

examples.en: Should I bring a jacket? — Yes, you should.
examples.id: Sebaiknya saya bawa jaket? — Ya, sebaiknya bawa.

id.title: should / shouldn't untuk memberi saran
id.explanation: should + kata kerja dasar dipakai untuk memberi saran (ide yang bagus); shouldn't (= should not) + kata kerja dasar artinya sesuatu itu ide yang buruk. should adalah kata bantu seperti can: tidak pernah berubah, tidak ada to sesudahnya, dan dalam pertanyaan ia diletakkan di depan tanpa do (Should I ...?).

keyPoints.title: have to / has to and must for obligation
keyPoints.explanation: Both mean 'harus': something is necessary. have to changes like the verb have: I / you / we / they have to, but he / she / it has to (like she has a car). must never changes and has no to after it: she must go. have to is the most common in speaking; must is common on signs and written rules.

examples.en: Rina has to take the KRL every day.
examples.id: Rina harus naik KRL setiap hari.

examples.en: We have to pay in cash here.
examples.id: Di sini kita harus bayar tunai.

id.title: have to / has to dan must untuk kewajiban
id.explanation: Keduanya berarti 'harus': sesuatu itu perlu dilakukan. have to berubah seperti kata kerja have: I / you / we / they have to, tapi he / she / it has to (seperti she has a car). must tidak pernah berubah dan tidak ada to sesudahnya: she must go. have to paling sering dipakai saat bicara; must sering muncul di papan tanda dan aturan tertulis.

keyPoints.title: mustn't (not allowed) vs don't have to (not necessary)
keyPoints.explanation: In negative sentences the meanings are very different. mustn't = it's not allowed (dilarang, tidak boleh): a rule or a danger. don't / doesn't have to = it's not necessary (tidak perlu, tidak harus): you can choose. Indonesian 'tidak harus' is don't have to, not mustn't.

examples.en: You mustn't use your phone in the exam.
The seminar is free. You don't have to pay.
examples.id: Seminarnya gratis. Kamu tidak perlu bayar.

examples.en: Sari doesn't have to cook tonight.
examples.id: Sari tidak perlu masak malam ini.

id.title: mustn't (dilarang) vs don't have to (tidak perlu)
id.explanation: Dalam kalimat negatif, artinya sangat berbeda. mustn't = tidak boleh, dilarang: ada aturan atau bahaya. don't / doesn't have to = tidak perlu, tidak harus: kamu boleh memilih. 'Tidak harus' dalam bahasa Indonesia artinya don't have to, bukan mustn't.

guidedPractice.prompt: Rina has a headache. Give her advice. Complete: You ___ take some medicine.
Dimas plays games until 2 a.m. every night, and he is always tired. Complete: You ___ play so late.
Complete with have to or has to: Budi ___ take the train to work every day.
guidedPractice.hint: Budi = he. Think of 'he has a car'.

guidedPractice.prompt: A sign in the library says: QUIET, PLEASE. Complete with mustn't or don't have to: You ___ talk loudly here.
guidedPractice.hint: It's a rule: talking loudly is not allowed.

independentPractice.prompt: Correct the mistake: You must to show your ticket.
independentPractice.hint: must works like can: no to after it.

independentPractice.prompt: It's Saturday and there's no school. Complete with mustn't or don't have to: The children ___ wake up early.
independentPractice.hint: Waking up early isn't forbidden. It just isn't necessary today.

independentPractice.prompt: Your friend wants to speak English better. Give one piece of advice with should.
expected: you should speak english every day
you should talk to native speakers

assessment.prompt: Your friend Budi has a bad cough, but he smokes every day. Give him advice with shouldn't. (Write a full sentence.)
acceptableAnswers: you should not smoke so much
you shouldn't smoke with a bad cough
assessment.rubric: Correct: You shouldn't / should not smoke (+ any sensible ending). 'You shouldn't to smoke' or 'You don't should smoke' = 50 (right idea, wrong form). 'You should smoke' = 0. 'You mustn't smoke' = 60 (too strong for friendly advice, and the item asks for shouldn't).

assessment.prompt: Correct the mistake: You should to see a doctor.
assessment.rubric: Correct: You should see a doctor (no to after should). Changing the meaning (e.g. 'You must see a doctor' or 'You have to see a doctor') = 50. Keeping 'to' = 0.

assessment.prompt: My sister is a nurse. Complete with have to or has to: She ___ work at night.
acceptableAnswers: she has to work at night
assessment.rubric: Correct: has to (she = he/she/it, like 'she has'). 'have to' = 0. 'must' = 70 (correct English, but the item asks for have to or has to).

assessment.prompt: A rule for ojek passengers. Put the words in the right order: wear / must / a helmet / you
assessment.rubric: Correct: You must wear a helmet. 'You must to wear a helmet' or 'You must wears a helmet' = 40. Wrong word order (e.g. 'Must you wear a helmet', which is a question) = 30.

assessment.prompt: A sign at a petrol station says: NO SMOKING. Complete with mustn't or don't have to: You ___ smoke here.
assessment.rubric: Correct: mustn't / must not (a rule: not allowed). 'can't' / 'cannot' = 80 (right meaning, but not one of the two words asked for). 'don't have to' = 0 (it would mean smoking is just not necessary).

assessment.prompt: Tomorrow is a public holiday, and the office is closed. Complete with mustn't or don't have to: We ___ go to work tomorrow.
acceptableAnswers: we don't have to go to work tomorrow
we do not have to go to work tomorrow
assessment.rubric: Correct: don't have to (not necessary: it's a holiday, not a rule against working). 'mustn't' = 0 (it would mean going to work is forbidden). 'doesn't have to' = 50 (right meaning, but we takes don't).

assessment.prompt: Dewi's office is very near her house. She can walk there. Complete with mustn't or doesn't have to: She ___ take a taxi.
acceptableAnswers: she doesn't have to take a taxi
she does not have to take a taxi
assessment.rubric: Correct: doesn't have to (not necessary: she can walk). 'doesn't has to' = 50 (right meaning, but after doesn't the verb is have). 'don't have to' = 60 (right meaning, but she takes doesn't). 'mustn't' = 0 (taking a taxi isn't forbidden).

blocks.text:
Use **should** to give advice: you think something is a **good idea**. Use **shouldn't** (= should not) when you think something is a **bad idea**. In Indonesian this is *sebaiknya* and *sebaiknya jangan*.

The pattern is **should / shouldn't + base verb**. The **base verb** is the verb as it is in the dictionary: no -s, no -ing, no to (*rest, go, eat, drink*).

id.text:
Pakai **should** untuk memberi saran: kamu merasa sesuatu itu **ide yang bagus**. Pakai **shouldn't** (= should not) kalau kamu merasa sesuatu itu **ide yang buruk**. Dalam bahasa Indonesia artinya *sebaiknya* dan *sebaiknya jangan*.

Polanya **should / shouldn't + kata kerja dasar**. **Kata kerja dasar** adalah kata kerja seperti di kamus: tanpa -s, tanpa -ing, tanpa to (*rest, go, eat, drink*).

rows.id: Sebaiknya kamu minum lebih banyak air.

rows.en: Your throat hurts. You shouldn't drink iced tea.
rows.id: Tenggorokanmu sakit. Sebaiknya jangan minum es teh.

rows.en: Budi should study for his test.
We shouldn't park here. It's a bus stop.
rows.id: Sebaiknya kita jangan parkir di sini. Ini halte bus.

blocks.text:
**No to, no -s.** *should* works like *can*: it's a helper word (a small word that helps the main verb), so it never changes, and the base verb comes straight after it. Say **You should rest**, not 'You should to rest'. Say **She should go**, not 'She shoulds go' or 'She should goes'.
Why do people add *to*? Because *have to* (later in this lesson) has a *to*. *should* doesn't.

id.text:
**Tanpa to, tanpa -s.** *should* bekerja seperti *can*: ia kata bantu (kata kecil yang membantu kata kerja utama), jadi tidak pernah berubah, dan kata kerja dasar langsung mengikutinya. Katakan **You should rest**, bukan 'You should to rest'. Katakan **She should go**, bukan 'She shoulds go' atau 'She should goes'.
Kenapa orang sering menambah *to*? Karena *have to* (nanti di pelajaran ini) memang punya *to*. *should* tidak.

blocks.text: **sebaiknya, not harus.** In Indonesian we often give a friend advice with *harus*: *Kamu harus istirahat!* In English, *You must rest* sounds very strong, like an order from a doctor. For friendly advice, use **should**: *You should go home and sleep.*

id.text: **sebaiknya, bukan harus.** Dalam bahasa Indonesia kita sering memberi saran ke teman dengan *harus*: *Kamu harus istirahat!* Dalam bahasa Inggris, *You must rest* terdengar sangat kuat, seperti perintah dokter. Untuk saran yang ramah, pakai **should**: *You should go home and sleep.*

blocks.prompt: Dimas has a test tomorrow. Which advice is correct?
blocks.explain: should + base verb: should study. No to after should, and no -s on the verb, even with he.

id.prompt: Dimas ada ujian besok. Saran mana yang benar?
id.explain: should + kata kerja dasar: should study. Tidak ada to sesudah should, dan kata kerjanya tanpa -s, walaupun subjeknya he.

material.title: have to, has to and must (harus)

blocks.text:
When something is **necessary** (a rule, your job, a timetable), use **have to** or **must** + base verb. Both mean *harus* or *wajib*.
- **have to** changes with the **subject** (who does it: *I, Rina, my boss*): **I / you / we / they have to**, but **he / she / it has to**.
- **must** never changes, like *can* and *should*: **I must, she must**. There's no *to* after must.

id.text:
Kalau sesuatu **perlu** dilakukan (aturan, pekerjaanmu, jadwal), pakai **have to** atau **must** + kata kerja dasar. Keduanya berarti *harus* atau *wajib*.
- **have to** berubah mengikuti **subjek** (siapa yang melakukan: *I, Rina, my boss*): **I / you / we / they have to**, tapi **he / she / it has to**.
- **must** tidak pernah berubah, seperti *can* dan *should*: **I must, she must**. Tidak ada *to* sesudah must.

blocks.text: **Why 'she has to'?** The *have* in *have to* is the normal verb *have* you know from the simple present: *I have a car*, but *she **has** a car*. It works the same way here: *I have to work*, but *she **has** to work*. So 'She have to work' is a mistake.

id.text: **Kenapa 'she has to'?** Kata *have* di *have to* adalah kata kerja *have* biasa yang sudah kamu kenal dari simple present: *I have a car*, tapi *she **has** a car*. Di sini caranya sama: *I have to work*, tapi *she **has** to work*. Jadi 'She have to work' itu salah.

rows.en: I have to start work at 8 a.m.
rows.id: Saya harus mulai kerja jam 8 pagi.

rows.en: Rina has to take the KRL every day.
rows.id: Rina harus naik KRL setiap hari.

rows.en: We have to pay in cash here.
rows.id: Di sini kita harus bayar tunai.

rows.en: I must call my mother tonight.
rows.id: Saya harus menelepon ibu saya nanti malam.

blocks.text:
**must or have to?** In these sentences both mean *harus*, and very often both are correct. A simple guide: **have to** is the most common when you speak (jobs, timetables, rules). **must** is common on signs and in written rules, and when *you* feel something is important (*I must call my mother*). Don't worry about the difference yet: get the form right first.
**Say it naturally:** in fast speech *have to* sounds like 'HAF-ta' and *has to* like 'HAS-ta'. Always write two words.

id.text:
**must atau have to?** Di kalimat-kalimat ini keduanya berarti *harus*, dan sering sekali keduanya benar. Panduan sederhana: **have to** paling sering dipakai saat bicara (pekerjaan, jadwal, aturan). **must** sering muncul di papan tanda dan aturan tertulis, dan saat *kamu sendiri* merasa sesuatu itu penting (*I must call my mother*). Belum perlu pusing soal bedanya: yang penting bentuknya benar dulu.
**Ucapkan dengan natural:** saat bicara cepat, *have to* terdengar seperti 'HAF-ta' dan *has to* seperti 'HAS-ta'. Tetap ditulis dua kata.

blocks.prompt: We ___ wear a uniform at school.
blocks.explain: We goes with have to (like we have). has to is only for he / she / it, and must never has to after it.

id.prompt: Lengkapi: We ___ wear a uniform at school.
id.explain: We berpasangan dengan have to (seperti we have). has to hanya untuk he / she / it, dan sesudah must tidak pernah ada to.

id.title: have to, has to dan must (harus)

material.title: mustn't (dilarang) vs don't have to (tidak perlu)

blocks.text:
In positive sentences, *must* and *have to* both mean *harus*. But in **negative** sentences they mean very different things!
- **mustn't** (= must not) = *dilarang, tidak boleh, jangan*. It's **not allowed**: there's a rule, or it's dangerous.
- **don't have to** = *tidak perlu, tidak harus, tidak usah*. It's **not necessary**: you can do it if you want, but you don't need to. With he / she / it: **doesn't have to**.

id.text:
Dalam kalimat positif, *must* dan *have to* sama-sama berarti *harus*. Tapi dalam kalimat **negatif**, artinya sangat berbeda!
- **mustn't** (= must not) = *dilarang, tidak boleh, jangan*. Artinya **tidak diizinkan**: ada aturan, atau berbahaya.
- **don't have to** = *tidak perlu, tidak harus, tidak usah*. Artinya **tidak perlu**: boleh kamu lakukan kalau mau, tapi tidak wajib. Untuk he / she / it: **doesn't have to**.

rows.en: You mustn't use your phone in the exam.
You mustn't touch the cables. It's dangerous.
The seminar is free. You don't have to pay.
rows.id: Seminarnya gratis. Kamu tidak perlu bayar.

rows.en: Sari doesn't have to cook tonight. Her mother is cooking.
rows.id: Sari tidak perlu masak malam ini. Ibunya sedang masak.

blocks.text: **The Indonesian trap: tidak harus is NOT mustn't.** Word by word, *tidak harus* looks like *must not*. But **mustn't** means *dilarang*! Imagine you invite a friend to your house and say 'You mustn't bring anything'. It sounds like a rule: bringing a gift is forbidden. You mean *tidak usah*: **You don't have to bring anything.**

id.text: **Jebakan bahasa Indonesia: tidak harus BUKAN mustn't.** Kalau diterjemahkan kata per kata, *tidak harus* kelihatannya *must not*. Padahal **mustn't** artinya *dilarang*! Bayangkan kamu mengundang teman ke rumah lalu bilang 'You mustn't bring anything'. Kedengarannya seperti aturan: dilarang membawa oleh-oleh. Maksudmu *tidak usah*: **You don't have to bring anything.**

blocks.text:
**doesn't have to, not 'doesn't has to'.** After *doesn't*, the verb goes back to its base form, as in the simple present (*She doesn't work*). So: **She doesn't have to go.** And *mustn't* never changes: *she mustn't*.
**Say it:** in *mustn't* the first t is silent: 'MAS-ent'.
**British and American:** *mustn't* is very common in British English. Americans usually say **must not** in written rules, or **can't** when they speak (*You can't park here*). You know *can't* for rules from the lesson on can: here it means the same as mustn't.

id.text:
**doesn't have to, bukan 'doesn't has to'.** Sesudah *doesn't*, kata kerjanya kembali ke bentuk dasar, seperti di simple present (*She doesn't work*). Jadi: **She doesn't have to go.** Dan *mustn't* tidak pernah berubah: *she mustn't*.
**Cara mengucapkan:** di *mustn't*, huruf t yang pertama tidak dibaca: 'MAS-ent'.
**British dan American:** *mustn't* sangat umum di bahasa Inggris British. Orang Amerika biasanya memakai **must not** di aturan tertulis, atau **can't** saat bicara (*You can't park here*). Kamu sudah kenal *can't* untuk aturan dari pelajaran can: di sini artinya sama dengan mustn't.

blocks.prompt: Budi has a lot of rice at home. He ___ buy rice today.
blocks.explain: Buying rice isn't forbidden; it just isn't necessary, so: doesn't have to. After doesn't the verb is have, not has.

id.prompt: Lengkapi: Budi has a lot of rice at home. He ___ buy rice today.
id.explain: Membeli beras tidak dilarang; hanya tidak perlu, jadi: doesn't have to. Sesudah doesn't, kata kerjanya have, bukan has.

blocks.prompt: A sign in a museum: DON'T TOUCH THE PAINTINGS. Visitors ___ touch the paintings.
blocks.explain: A sign with a rule means it's not allowed: mustn't. don't have to would mean touching is just not necessary.

id.prompt: Papan di museum: DON'T TOUCH THE PAINTINGS. Lengkapi: Visitors ___ touch the paintings.
id.explain: Papan berisi aturan artinya tidak boleh: mustn't. don't have to artinya menyentuh itu hanya tidak perlu.

material.title: Asking for advice and about rules

blocks.text:
To ask for advice, put **should** first: **Should I** + base verb? (*Sebaiknya saya …?*). There's no *do*, just like *Can I …?*.
To ask if something is necessary, use **Do / Does … have to …?** (*Apakah saya harus …?*). *have to* works like a normal verb, so it needs *do / does*, like *Do you have a car?*.
Questions with must (*Must I …?*) sound old-fashioned, so say **Do I have to …?**.

id.text:
Untuk minta saran, letakkan **should** di depan: **Should I** + kata kerja dasar? (*Sebaiknya saya …?*). Tidak pakai *do*, sama seperti *Can I …?*.
Untuk bertanya apakah sesuatu wajib, pakai **Do / Does … have to …?** (*Apakah saya harus …?*). *have to* bekerja seperti kata kerja biasa, jadi perlu *do / does*, seperti *Do you have a car?*.
Pertanyaan dengan must (*Must I …?*) terdengar kuno, jadi pakai **Do I have to …?**.

rows.en: Should I bring a jacket? — Yes, you should. It's cold in the office.
rows.id: Sebaiknya saya bawa jaket? — Ya. Di kantor dingin.

rows.en: Should I call him now? — No, you shouldn't. It's very late.
rows.id: Sebaiknya saya telepon dia sekarang? — Jangan. Sudah malam sekali.

rows.en: Do I have to pay for parking? — Yes, you do. It's 5,000 rupiah.
rows.id: Apakah saya harus bayar parkir? — Ya. Rp5.000.

rows.en: Does Sari have to work on Saturday? — No, she doesn't.
rows.id: Apakah Sari harus kerja hari Sabtu? — Tidak.

blocks.prompt: You want to know if the toilet at the station is free. Which question is correct?
blocks.explain: Questions about what's necessary use Do + subject + have to + base verb. After do, use have (not has), and there's never a to after must.

id.prompt: Kamu mau tahu apakah toilet di stasiun gratis. Pertanyaan mana yang benar?
id.explain: Pertanyaan tentang apa yang wajib memakai Do + subjek + have to + kata kerja dasar. Sesudah do, pakai have (bukan has), dan sesudah must tidak pernah ada to.
